items.title: Successful Treatment of Pembrolizumab-associated Myositis-myocarditis-myasthenia Gravis Overlap Syndrome with Gastrointestinal Pseudo-obstruction Using Zilucoplan: A Case Report.
items.authors: Hiroki Komatsu, Minako Yamada, Ken Wako, Yuki Nagasako, Yusuke Sugiyama, Taro Bannai
items.abstract: Myositis-myocarditis-myasthenia gravis (MMM) overlap syndrome is a rare, potentially fatal complication of immune checkpoint inhibitor (ICI) therapy. We report a 74-year-old man with pre-existing thymoma and anti-acetylcholine receptor antibody positivity who developed pembrolizumab-induced MMM complicated by gastrointestinal pseudo-obstruction (GIPO). Despite the administration of corticosteroids and intravenous immunoglobulin, ocular symptoms persisted, and bowel dysmotility progressed. We initiated zilucoplan, a complement C5 inhibitor. Within days, diplopia and dysphagia resolved, and GIPO markedly improved on radiography, enabling oral intake. To our knowledge, this is the first case of pembrolizumab-induced MMM treated with zilucoplan and the first ICI-mediated GIPO managed with a complement inhibitor.

items.title: Immune checkpoint inhibitor-induced myocarditis, myositis, and myasthenia crisis overlap syndrome and mortality: a pooled case analysis.
items.authors: Madhumita Kolluri, Kerry S Singh, Mira Hasan, Mohamed A Jailani, Shea-Lee Godin, Hossam A Mohammed
items.abstract: Cancer patients on immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICIs) can rarely develop concurrent myocarditis, myositis, and myasthenia gravis, known as 3M syndrome. While a few reviews have been published to better understand the characteristics of 3M patients, no study to date has identified predictors of mortality in these patients. We systematically reviewed five databases for published cases of 3M syndrome from 2014 to 2024. Of 113 articles, we identified 153 adult 3M patients. For each patient, we recorded demographic data, ICI regimen, symptoms, diagnostic findings, treatment modalities, and discharge outcomes. Using multivariable logistic regression, we compared variables by mortality. Patients had a median age of 72 years, were predominantly male (73%), and were diagnosed with melanoma (32%). Pembrolizumab (30%) was the most common ICI. Common symptoms were dyspnea (59%), muscle weakness (59%), and dysphagia (37%), and most (73%) had varying degree ocular involvement. Troponin and creatinine kinase were elevated in nearly all patients. We identified three characteristics related to mortality: older age ( P = 0.005), elevated liver enzymes ( P = 0.02), and intubation ( P = 0.002). We also identified factors related to survival: treatment with rituximab ( P = 0.04) or abatacept ( P = 0.02), elevated lactate dehydrogenase ( P = 0.03), and tracheostomy ( P = 0.046). Further investigation into potential predictors of survival in 3M syndrome patients, particularly regarding rituximab and abatacept use, may improve patient care and outcomes.

items.title: Controversies and consensus on immune function and long-term health risks following adult thymectomy: a comprehensive review of molecular mechanisms and real-world evidence.
items.authors: Pile Zhao, Xiumei Li, Xueqin Wang, Tongzhen Xu, Hengxiao Lu
items.abstract: To evaluate the long-term immunological, oncological, and clinical consequences of adult thymectomy by synthesizing recent basic, translational, and real-world clinical evidence. Historical surgical paradigms regarded the post-pubertal adult thymus as an immunologically redundant, fatty involuted organ, justifying routine "incidental" resection during cardiac procedures. A high-profile 2023 cohort study in The New England Journal of Medicine (NEJM) challenged this concept, reporting that adult thymectomy significantly increased 5-year all-cause mortality and cancer risk. Subsequent population-level studies (US SEER/NCDB, French PMSI) and deep-learning imaging cohorts have sparked debate, offering both corroborating and conflicting insights into adult thymic function. This review synthesizes cellular mechanisms (TREC dynamics, TCR repertoire contraction, senescence-associated T cells, Treg lineage stability) and endocrine factors (thymulin-mediated myeloid regulation) with clinical data stratified by age at surgery, indication, resection extent, and follow-up duration. The adult thymus remains functionally active, exporting naïve T cells and humoral immunomodulators like thymulin that maintain peripheral immune tolerance and restrain inflammaging. Clinical evaluation must differentiate between incidental resection (which induces avoidable iatrogenic immunosenescence) and therapeutic resection (e.g., for thymic epithelial tumors or myasthenia gravis), where removing a diseased, immunosuppressive microenvironment can reduce secondary cancer risk. Partial thymectomy (PT) is emerging as an option to preserve immunocompetence when oncologically feasible.
items.zhSummary: 本文综述了成人胸腺切除术后长期免疫学、肿瘤学及临床影响，整合基础、转化及真实世界临床证据。传统观点认为成年胸腺功能退化，可在心脏手术中偶发切除。但2023年的高影响力队列研究发现，成人胸腺切除后五年全因死亡率及癌症风险升高，引发学界争议。文章汇总了细胞机制与内分泌因素，强调成年胸腺仍有功能，分泌新生T细胞及胸腺素以维持免疫耐受和抑制炎症老化。临床需区分偶发切除与治疗性切除，后者可能降低继发癌风险。部分切除术作为保留免疫功能的选项正在被探索。

items.title: [Can the response to intravenous immunoglobulins be predicted during a first exacerbation of generalized myasthenia gravis?].
items.authors: Matthias Dion, Antoine Gavoille, Valérie Chamouard, Antoine Pegat, Françoise Bouhour
items.abstract: Intravenous immunoglobulins (IVIg), together with plasma exchange (PLEX), remain one of the standard treatments for acute worsening of generalized autoimmune myasthenia gravis, including myasthenic exacerbations and myasthenic crises, the latter representing the most severe form of disease deterioration. In a context marked by the emergence of new targeted therapies, particularly neonatal Fc receptor (FcRn) inhibitors and complement inhibitors (CI), as well as recurrent shortages of IVIg supply, the ability to identify patients who are likely or unlikely to respond to IVIg has become a major clinical challenge. We retrospectively analysed a cohort of 93 patients who received IVIg during a first myasthenic exacerbation or crisis. Clinical improvement was observed in 87% of patients. No clinical, biological, electrophysiological, or disease-history-related factor was significantly associated with a poorer treatment response. These findings confirm the overall effectiveness of IVIg and support their continued role as a first-line treatment for acute worsening in generalized myasthenia gravis. Peut-on prédire la réponse aux immunoglobulines intraveineuses lors d'une première exacerbation de myasthénie généralisée ? Les immunoglobulines intraveineuses (IgIV) constituent, avec les échanges plasmatiques (EP), l'un des traitements de référence des aggravations aiguës de la myasthénie auto-immune généralisée, qu'il s'agisse d'exacerbations ou de crises myasthéniques, ces dernières représentant les formes les plus sévères. Dans un contexte marqué par l'émergence de nouvelles thérapeutiques ciblées, notamment les inhibiteurs du récepteur néonatal des immunoglobulines G (FcRn) et les inhibiteurs du complément (IC), ainsi que par des tensions récurrentes d'approvisionnement en IgIV, la capacité à identifier les patients susceptibles de répondre ou non à ce traitement devient un enjeu majeur. Nous avons analysé rétrospectivement une cohorte de 93 patients ayant reçu des IgIV lors d'une première exacerbation ou d'une première crise myasthénique. Une amélioration clinique a été observée chez 87% d'entre eux. Aucun facteur clinique, biologique, électrophysiologique ou lié à l'histoire de la maladie n'a été associé de manière significative à une moindre réponse au traitement. Ces résultats confirment l'efficacité globale des IgIV et confortent leur place comme traitement de première intention des aggravations aiguës de la myasthénie généralisée.

items.title: Ocular Myasthenia Gravis Unmasking Molecularly High-Risk but Clinically Indolent Chronic Lymphocytic Leukemia: A Case Report.
items.authors: Haider Bin Khalid, Muhammad Furqan, Zain Ul Abedin, Mehwish Saleem, Mata-E-Alla Dogar, Maryam Saqib
items.abstract: We report a patient who presented with acute-onset diplopia and fatigable ptosis, subsequently diagnosed with Myasthenia Gravis based on elevated acetylcholine receptor antibodies. Neuroimaging and chest imaging were unremarkable, excluding structural causes and thymoma. During evaluation, persistent lymphocytosis prompted further hematologic workup, which confirmed early-stage Chronic Lymphocytic Leukemia with trisomy 12 and a TP53 mutation. The patient received pyridostigmine and a tapering course of corticosteroids, resulting in rapid clinical improvement and complete resolution of ocular symptoms. The leukemia remained asymptomatic and was managed conservatively with a watchful waiting approach. The clinical course was favorable with sustained remission of myasthenia gravis off therapy and stable hematologic parameters on follow-up. This case highlights the diagnostic interplay between autoimmune and lymphoproliferative disorders and underscores the importance of a multidisciplinary approach in managing such overlapping clinical entities.

items.title: First Reported Coexistence of Acetylcholine Receptor-Positive Myasthenia Gravis and Genetically Confirmed Spinocerebellar Ataxia Type 6.
items.authors: Jawad Abou Zeid, Kedrick Shin, Patrick Sleiman, Saniya Ahmed, Asma Zitouni, Lisle Blackbourn
items.abstract: When a patient with a long-standing neurological diagnosis develops new symptoms, those symptoms are frequently attributed to the disease that is already known, and a second, unrelated disorder may remain unrecognized for years. We describe a patient in whom myasthenia gravis (MG) and spinocerebellar ataxia type 6 (SCA6) occurred together, a combination that has not, to our knowledge, been previously reported. A 57-year-old man with acetylcholine receptor antibody-positive MG diagnosed in 1983 presented with progressive imbalance despite largely stable MG symptoms. His MG remained well controlled on low-dose prednisone and pyridostigmine following thymectomy, with intermittent azathioprine therapy. Neurological examination demonstrated cerebellar signs including dysmetria, dysdiadochokinesia, gaze-evoked nystagmus, and dysarthria. Brain MRI showed atrophy of the cerebellar hemispheres and vermis with associated brainstem volume loss. Extensive evaluation for acquired causes of cerebellar ataxia/degeneration, including paraneoplastic and autoimmune antibody testing, was unrevealing. Progressive ataxia continued despite largely stable neuromuscular symptoms. Family history revealed ataxia in his father and a similar disorder in his identical twin brother. Several years before the diagnosis was established, he experienced an MG exacerbation with bulbar and generalized weakness that responded to plasmapheresis. Genetic testing subsequently identified a pathogenic CACNA1A CAG repeat expansion of 22 repeats, confirming SCA6, just over a decade after the initial onset of his ataxia symptoms and establishing the coexistence of two distinct and rare neurological disorders. This case highlights the diagnostic challenge of evaluating new neurological symptoms in patients with established chronic, rare neurological disease. Progressive cerebellar dysfunction was initially overshadowed by the patient's longstanding MG, resulting in delayed recognition of a hereditary ataxia. Clinicians should maintain a broad differential diagnosis when symptoms evolve in a manner that is atypical for the known disease process. Recognition of coexisting neurological disorders is essential for accurate diagnosis, prognostication, genetic counseling, and multidisciplinary management. Coexistence of an acquired neuromuscular disorder and a hereditary cerebellar ataxia is possible; antibody testing to exclude an acquired ataxia and genetic confirmation of the inherited disorder are both required, and recognition of both diagnoses directly informs immunotherapy decisions, rehabilitation, and family counselling.

items.title: Surgery for Nonthymomatous Myasthenia Gravis.
items.authors: Melek Ağkoç, Erica Pietroluongo, Cecilia Pompili
items.abstract: Myasthenia gravis (MG) is an autoimmune disorder characterized by fluctuating muscle weakness due to impaired neuromuscular transmission, most commonly mediated by antibodies against the acetylcholine receptor. The thymus plays a central role in disease pathogenesis, and complete thymectomy including all thymic and mediastinal adipose tissue has been shown to improve outcomes in patients with nonthymomatous, antiacetylcholine receptor antibody positive generalized MG. Minimally invasive approaches, including video-assisted and robotic-assisted thymectomy, offer remission rates comparable to open surgery with reduced perioperative morbidity. Careful patient selection and perioperative disease optimization remain essential.

items.title: Improvement of anti-muscle-specific receptor tyrosine kinase antibody-positive myasthenia gravis with dysphagia after combination immunotherapy: A case report.
items.authors: Takayuki Handa, Eri Takeshita, Toshiyuki Yamamoto, Yuko Shimizu-Motohashi, Keiko Ishigaki, Yumi Sato
items.abstract: In adult patients, anti-muscle-specific receptor tyrosine kinase antibody-positive myasthenia gravis (MuSK-MG) frequently presents with bulbar symptoms and tends to progress to myasthenic crisis, although data in pediatric patients are limited. Pediatric-onset MuSK-MG is rare, and a standard treatment approach has not been established. Here, we report a pediatric-onset case of MuSK-MG in which combination immunotherapy improved symptoms, including dysphagia. A 15-year-old girl presented with diplopia that had begun 2 years prior, followed by gradual worsening of dysphagia and dysarthria. A videofluoroscopic swallowing study (VFSS) demonstrated inadequate soft palate elevation, poor pharyngeal contraction, repeated swallowing, laryngeal penetration, and residue in the epiglottic vallecula and pyriform sinus. She tested positive for anti-muscle-specific receptor tyrosine kinase antibodies (anti-MuSK antibodies) and was diagnosed with MuSK-MG. Treatment with intravenous immunoglobulin, intravenous methylprednisolone, and oral prednisolone and tacrolimus led to improvement in her symptoms, including dysphagia, starting 3 weeks after initiation. MuSK-MG may be responsive to treatment even 2 years after symptom onset. Anti-MuSK antibodies testing should be considered in patients with progressive dysphagia and dysarthria, particularly when bulbar symptoms are unexplained. VFSS was useful for objectively assessing the severity of dysphagia and its improvement.

items.title: HLA profiles in immune checkpoint inhibitor-associated neuromuscular adverse events.
items.authors: Ayal Rozenberg, Esther Ganelin-Cohen, Lilach Gutter Kapon, Shany Guly Gofrit, Alexandra Amiel, Gal Tsur
items.abstract: Immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICIs) can cause neuromuscular adverse events (nmAEs), yet the immunogenetic background of affected patients remains poorly characterized. We descriptively characterized the HLA profile of patients with ICI-associated nmAEs at two tertiary Israeli centers and explored allele and multilocus allele patterns relative to available population references. Eight-locus HLA typing was performed in 17 consecutive patients with ICI-associated nmAEs. Allele and carrier frequencies were descriptively compared with available Israeli and Mediterranean/European population references. Because the study lacked an ancestry-matched ICI-treated control cohort, these comparisons were considered exploratory and hypothesis-generating. Six patients had myasthenia gravis (MG), five had myositis, and six had overlap syndromes; median age at onset was 76 years (IQR 72 to 80). HLA-DQA1 05:05 was present in 10/17 patients (58.8%) compared with 19.0% in the reference population ( OR 6.09, 95% CI 2.31 to 16.04, p<0.001, q=0.008 ). DQB1 03:01 was present in 10/17 patients (58.8%). DRB1 11-DQA1 05:05-DQB1 03:01 multilocus allele combination was observed in 9/17 patients (52.9%). HLA-B 35 and C 04:01 co-occurred in 7/17 patients (41.2%). DRB1 11 carrier status was not significantly associated with cardiac involvement (7/9 vs. 4/8, p=0.335) or mortality (4/9 vs. 1/8, p=0.294). This small descriptive cohort identified recurrent HLA class II allele patterns among patients with ICI-associated neuromuscular adverse events, most prominently DQA1 05:05 and its frequent co-occurrence with DQB1 03:01 and DRB1*11. These findings are exploratory and cannot distinguish susceptibility to ICI-associated neuromuscular toxicity from a broader predisposition to neuromuscular autoimmunity or population structure. Validation in larger, ancestry-matched cohorts including ICI-treated patients without immune-related adverse events is required.

items.title: Association Between Myasthenia Gravis and Sarcoidosis: A Case Report.
items.authors: Maryam Amanahou, Mohamed Laghdaf Maouelainin, Abdellah Taous, Abdelfatah Zidane, Naji Amrani Hicham
items.abstract: Sarcoidosis is a systemic granulomatous disease of unknown cause. Its association with myasthenia gravis has mainly been documented in isolated case reports and small series. We report double-seronegative myasthenia gravis for the antibodies tested, associated with stage I thoracic sarcoidosis and thymic hyperplasia without thymoma. A 46-year-old woman was hospitalized in November 2021 for grade 3 exertional dyspnea according to the modified Medical Research Council scale, associated with fluctuating left-sided ptosis that worsened toward the end of the day. The neostigmine test was positive, with transient improvement in the ptosis. Low-frequency repetitive nerve stimulation demonstrated a decrement compatible with a postsynaptic neuromuscular transmission disorder. Antibodies against the acetylcholine receptor and anti-MuSK antibodies were negative, leading to the diagnosis of double-seronegative myasthenia gravis for the antibodies tested. At the same time, thoracic imaging showed multiple bilateral mediastinal and hilar lymphadenopathies without pulmonary parenchymal involvement. Mediastinoscopy with lymph node biopsy revealed non-necrotizing epithelioid and giant-cell granulomatous lymphadenitis compatible with sarcoidosis. Systemic corticosteroid therapy with prednisone was initiated. The neurological course was marked by worsening myasthenic manifestations, with increased ptosis, diplopia, painful dysphagia, and predominantly left-sided weakness. A course of intravenous immunoglobulin resulted in marked clinical improvement. Thymectomy performed in July 2023 revealed thymic hyperplasia without thymoma. At the latest available follow-up, the patient was asymptomatic and remained under neurological follow-up. The coexistence of sarcoidosis and myasthenia gravis remains rarely described. In this case, the two diagnoses were supported by independent findings. Sarcoidosis was supported by radiological and histological findings, whereas the fluctuating and fatigable nature of the ptosis, the response to neostigmine, and the electrophysiological abnormalities supported the diagnosis of myasthenia gravis. Neurosarcoidosis was the main neurological differential diagnosis. The coexistence of the two diseases may be coincidental and, although an immune-mediated background may be considered, the available data do not demonstrate a specific or causal relationship between sarcoidosis and myasthenia gravis. This case describes a rare association between stage I thoracic sarcoidosis and double-seronegative myasthenia gravis, with thymic hyperplasia without thymoma. It highlights the importance of documenting each condition separately and of investigating a neuromuscular transmission abnormality in the presence of fluctuating ptosis, diplopia, or bulbar involvement in a patient with sarcoidosis, rather than immediately attributing these manifestations to neurosarcoidosis.

items.title: Myogenic carbonic anhydrase 3 suppresses intracellular complement C3a-mediated follicular helper T cell differentiation in myasthenia gravis.
items.authors: Shiqian Huang, Xiaonan Zhao, Hong Zhou, Xiang Miao, Fulvio Baggi, Jin Wu
items.abstract: Myasthenia gravis is generally regarded as an autoantibody-mediated autoimmune disease, while whether myogenic factors trigger this immune disorder remains elusive. Our previous studies identified carbonic anhydrase 3 (CAR3) that is significantly downregulated in muscles from myasthenia gravis patients and plays an essential role in myasthenia gravis pathogenesis. In the present study, using experimental autoimmune myasthenia gravis (EAMG) mouse model generated with muscle specific Car3 deficient (Acta1 cre Car3 f/f ) mice, we found that Car3 deficiency in muscle considerably exacerbated myasthenia symptoms. Importantly, EAMG Acta1 cre Car3 f/f mice exhibited substantial T follicular helper (T FH ) differentiation in muscle and significantly elevated levels of anti-AChR autoantibodies. Additionally, we detected increased intracellular complement C3a in Car3 deficient muscle cells. RNA-seq analysis and genetic validation experiments illustrated that Car3 deficiency facilitates intracellular C3a production via cathepsin S. Once released, myogenic C3a binds to C3a receptor on T cells, thereby driving T FH differentiation and subsequent autoantibody production. Collectively, our results demonstrate that Car3 deficiency promotes intracellular C3 activation in muscle cells and induces T FH differentiation, revealing a critical role of muscle-immune communication in the pathogenesis of myasthenia gravis.

items.title: Cross-Sectional Serological Profile Anti-AChR by ELISA of a Brazilian Cohort of Patients With Suspected Myasthenia Gravis.
items.authors: Lucas Grobério Moulim de Moraes, Manoella Guerra de Albuquerque Bueno, Amanda Vitoria Freire de Oliveira, Giuliana França Teixeira Mandia Grossi, Milena Bongiorno Levignali, Carolina Lavigne Moreira
items.abstract: Myasthenia gravis (MG) is most commonly mediated by antibodies against the acetylcholine receptor (AChR). Although radioimmunoprecipitation assay (RIPA) is the reference standard, enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA) is widely used in routine practice, particularly in low- and middle-income settings, despite moderate sensitivity. We retrospectively reviewed patients investigated for suspected myasthenic syndromes who underwent anti-AChR IgG testing by ELISA between 2017 and 2025 at a tertiary MG center in Brazil. Demographic, clinical, electrophysiological, and serological data were analyzed. Diagnostic performance was assessed using receiver operating characteristic (ROC) analysis and multivariable logistic regression. Associations between antibody status and titers with MG phenotype, MGFA class, and MG-ADL scores were evaluated. Among 321 individuals, 212 (66.0%) were diagnosed with MG. Anti-AChR positivity was strongly associated with MG (p < 0.001), with observed sensitivity of 64.9% and specificity of 98.2%. Overall discriminative performance was high (area under the curve [AUC] 0.844). Antibody titers were significantly higher in MG versus non-MG patients (p < 0.001) and in generalized versus ocular MG. Seropositivity was more frequent in very late-onset (LO) MG (p = 0.001). Ocular and bulbar presentations and non-Caucasian ethnicity were independently associated with MG; repetitive nerve stimulation positivity showed the strongest association, although this is partly attributable to its inclusion in the diagnostic definition. Antibody positivity correlated with greater disease severity (MGFA ≥ IIb and higher MG-ADL scores), although correlations between titers and severity were modest. Immunotherapy was not associated with reduced seropositivity. Anti-AChR ELISA showed excellent specificity and good diagnostic discrimination, with moderate sensitivity in this real-world cohort. Because ELISA-negative samples were not retested by RIPA or cell-based assays (CBAs), this sensitivity should not be extrapolated to anti-AChR antibody testing overall.

Following acute stabilization, optimal maintenance immunotherapy remains uncertain in some patients. To evaluate the efficacy and safety of telitacicept as add-on treatment after antibody depletion therapy in patients with MC. A retrospective, non-randomized, single-center exploratory cohort study. We retrospectively reviewed patients with MC treated after antibody depletion therapy at a single center between November 2022 and February 2023. Patients receiving add-on telitacicept plus conventional immunotherapy were compared with patients who received conventional immunotherapy alone. Efficacy was assessed by using changes from baseline in Myasthenia Gravis Activities of Daily Living (MG-ADL) and Quantitative Myasthenia Gravis (QMG) scores, hospitalization-related outcomes, prednisone-equivalent dose, and safety. Eleven patients were enrolled. At months 1, 3, 6, and 12, median MG-ADL and QMG scores for both groups progressively decreased. No statistically significant differences were observed between groups for either score at any time point ( p all > 0.05). A numerical trend towards greater reduction in MG-ADL and QMG scores was noted in the T-group from month 6 to month 12. No significant inter-group differences were found in median length of ICU stay, duration of MV, or length of hospitalization ( p all > 0.05). Prednisone dose was lower in the telitacicept group during early follow-up, but no significant between-group difference was observed at 12 months ( p > 0.05). No medication-related serious adverse events, allergic reactions, or infections were documented in either group during treatment or follow-up. In this small retrospective exploratory cohort, no statistically significant inter-group differences were observed between telitacicept add-on therapy and conventional immunosuppression across the measured outcomes. Telitacicept may represent a potential strategy for long-term disease control after (MC), but these findings are hypothesis-generating and require confirmation in larger prospective studies. Why was this study done? Myasthenia gravis is a long-term disease in which the immune system attacks the connection between nerves and muscles. This can cause muscle weakness, drooping eyelids, and difficulty speaking, swallowing, or breathing. A myasthenic crisis is a life-threatening worsening of myasthenia gravis, when breathing muscles become so weak that the patient needs care in an intensive care unit (ICU) and help from a breathing machine (mechanical ventilation). Standard treatments can control a crisis, but it is still difficult to keep patients in long-term remission.Telitacicept is a newer immune treatment that blocks signals needed for producing harmful antibodies. We wanted to see whether adding telitacicept to usual treatment during myasthenic crisis might help. What did the researchers do? We studied 11 patients with myasthenic crisis. Some patients received telitacicept in addition to conventional immunosuppressive treatment (T-group). Others received conventional immunosuppression alone (C-group). We followed them for 12 months. We measured symptoms using a questionnaire about daily activities (MG-ADL) and a doctor’s assessment of muscle strength (QMG). We also recorded the length of mechanical ventilation, intensive care unit stay, hospital stay, and changes in prednisone dose. What did the researchers find? In both groups, MG-ADL and QMG scores improved steadily over 12 months, meaning patients generally became stronger and had fewer symptoms. There were no clear differences between groups at any time point. From month 6 to month 12, there was a numerical trend toward greater improvement in the telitacicept group, but this small study could not prove a definite advantage. ICU stay, ventilation time, hospital stay, and prednisone tapering were similar in both groups. What do these results mean? In this small group of patients with myasthenic crisis, adding telitacicept to standard treatment worked about as well as conventional.

items.title: Long‑term disease control in generalized myasthenia gravis: a systematic literature review.
items.authors: C Casasnovas, K G Claeys, F Saccà, T Verbiest, C Gary, W Noel
items.abstract: Generalized myasthenia gravis (gMG) is an autoimmune disease, causing impaired muscle contraction and weakness with a debilitating impact on quality of life. Despite a range of established treatment options, long-term outcomes in people with gMG remain poorly understood. A systematic literature review (SLR) was conducted to identify evidence for long-term (> 1 year) disease control and remission in adults with gMG from observational studies published from 2000 onwards. This analysis focused on a subset of publications reporting data for ≥ 1 gMG disease states defined as remission, minimal manifestations (MMs), or change in status. In total, 67 publications from the SLR reported data for ≥ 1 disease states. There was heterogeneity across included studies in terms of disease characteristics, reported treatments, outcomes definitions, and follow-up approaches, which were reflected in outcome reporting variability. No clear trends based on changed disease state over time were observed, however the proportion of patients achieving key clinical goals was generally low. Notably, complete stable remission (CSR), pharmacological remission (PR), and uncategorized remission achievement rates did not exceed 10, 30, and 50%, respectively, at any follow-up timepoint in most studies. Similarly, the proportion of patients achieving MM status, as measured by MM-0, MM-1, and MM-2, remained below 5, 20, and 20%, respectively, across most studies. These results suggest that at least 50% of gMG patients experience persistent symptoms over many years of follow-up. The lack of any trends in improving disease status over time suggests that patients are unable to optimally manage their disease with current treatment options. The protocol for this systematic review has been registered in PROSPERO (CRD420250641579).

items.title: Clinical and treatment profiles of myasthenic crisis patients in a tertiary hospital in the Philippines: a single-center retrospective study.
items.authors: Safrollah M Guinal, Mykha Marie B Tabuzo, Christian Wilson R Turalde
items.abstract: Myasthenic crisis is a life-threatening complication of myasthenia gravis. Data on its clinical profile and outcomes in resource-limited settings are limited. A retrospective review of pediatric and adult myasthenic crisis patients admitted at Philippine General Hospital from 2015 to 2024 was conducted. Sociodemographic, clinical, treatment, and outcome data were extracted from inpatient charts. Descriptive statistics and Pearson's chi-square, Fisher's exact, Wilcoxon rank-sum, and Kruskal-Wallis tests were used to analyze associations between clinical characteristics and outcomes. Eighty-two patients were included, mostly female (n = 49, 59.8%) with peak onset in the third decade. Infection was the leading precipitant of crisis, while hypertension, diabetes, and tuberculosis were common comorbidities. Nearly all required ventilation (96.3%, median nine days). Mortality was 13.4% (n = 11), mainly due to sepsis and respiratory failure. Younger age (< 30 years, p = 0.021) was linked to improved survival, whereas absence of intravenous immunoglobulin (IVIG) or therapeutic plasma exchange (TPE) was associated with higher mortality (p = 0.012). This study provided one of the largest descriptions of myasthenic crisis in the Philippines, demonstrating that infection remains the predominant inciting factor and timely rescue immunotherapy is associated with improved survival. These findings support strengthening access to specialized neuromuscular care and crisis-directed therapies in resource-constrained settings.

items.title: Assessing the Degree of Patient-Physician Agreement on Perceived Disease Burden in Generalised Myasthenia Gravis: A European Study.
items.authors: Lauren Halliwell, Alisa Matei, Elise Roche, Sophie Lehnerer
items.abstract: Generalised myasthenia gravis (gMG) significantly affects physical functioning and emotional wellbeing. Many patients with gMG report a disconnect between their lived experience and physicians' perceptions of disease impact, which may impact treatment priorities and shared decision-making. We assessed patient-physician concordance on perceived gMG burden and explored factors contributing to perceptual gaps. Across five European countries (France, Germany, Italy, Spain, UK), 167 adult patients with gMG and their treating physicians (n = 24) independently completed online surveys assessing the perceived impact of gMG on physical functioning and emotional wellbeing, using 0-100 visual analogue scales (VAS). Discordance was defined as an absolute VAS score difference of ≥ 20 points. Additionally, 25 patients and 25 physicians participated in semi-structured qualitative interviews exploring lived experiences, consultation dynamics, and treatment decision-making. VAS score agreement was assessed using intraclass correlation coefficient (ICC) and Bland-Altman analysis; qualitative interviews were analysed thematically. Overall, mean patient and physician VAS scores were similar for physical functioning (57.9 vs 59.6, p = 0.20) and emotional wellbeing (58.7 vs 61.0, p = 0.09), with "substantial" concordance in 81% of patient-physician pairs (ICC: ~ 0.7). Conversely, 19% of patient-physician pairs demonstrated clear discordance, with physicians either over- or underestimating burden. Notably, even among concordant pairs, up to one fifth reported score differences approaching the discordance threshold, reflecting subtle, but potentially meaningful, misalignment. Qualitative insights suggested that short consultations, under-recognition of fluctuating symptoms, and blind spots regarding psychosocial impacts may contribute to perceptual gaps. Despite overall broad patient-physician concordance of VAS scores, meaningful misalignment in perceived gMG burden persists. Qualitative insights highlighted perceptual gaps that may be driven by limited consultation time and under-addressed psychosocial needs. Incorporating structured, symptom-focused dialogue alongside standard assessments may improve recognition of disease burden and support patient-centred gMG management. Symptoms of generalised myasthenia gravis (gMG) can change daily and may affect education, work, social activities, travel, relationships, and emotional wellbeing. This study explored whether people with gMG and their doctors had similar views about gMG's impact. Researchers surveyed 167 people with gMG and their doctors across five European countries. Patients and doctors independently rated the impact of gMG on physical functioning and emotional wellbeing using a 0–100 scoring system, known as the visual analogue scale (VAS). Researchers also interviewed 25 patients and 25 doctors about their perspectives. Most patients and doctors gave similar VAS scores, suggesting a broadly shared understanding of gMG's impact. However, there were still small, but potentially meaningful, score differences, suggesting differences in perception that could be missed during an appointment. A larger gap was seen in almost a fifth of patient-doctor pairs. These pairs had VAS score differences of 20 points or more, meaning their perceptions of disease burden differed substantially. Doctors underestimated impact more often than they overestimated it. The interviews helped explain why these perception gaps may occur. Patients described challenges that were not always discussed during appointments, including fluctuating symptoms and the emotional and social effects of gMG. Doctors recognised these issues but said limited consultation time and assessment approaches make them difficult to capture. These findings highlight the importance of open conversations between patients and doctors to ensure that patients are heard and the full impact of gMG is recognised when making treatment decisions.

items.title: Sleep Related Breathing Disorders in Patients With MuSK Myasthenia Gravis, Compared to MuSK Negative Myasthenia Gravis.
items.authors: Bradley V Vaughn, Shakeel Tabish, James F Howard
items.abstract: Autoimmune Myasthenia Gravis (MG) is associated with obstructive sleep apnea. Muscle-specific kinase antibody positive MG (MuSK-ab+ gMG) patients often have more bulbar weakness than MuSK antibody negative (MuSK-ab-) patients, but data comparing sleep-related breathing disorders is scarce. Utilizing the University of North Carolina Myasthenia Gravis Registry, 30 MuSK-ab+ generalized MG (gMG) patients (26 female, 4 male) were matched with 30 MuSK-ab- gMG patients for age, sex, and Myasthenia Gravis Foundation of America (MGFA) clinical class. Additionally, 30 MuSK-ab- ocular MG patients were matched for age and sex. Features of sleep-related symptoms, sleep diagnosis, polysomnogram findings, need for positive airway pressure (PAP) and chronic nocturnal supplemental oxygen were analyzed. Statistical significance was determined using Chi-square test with 95% confidence intervals and Student T test (p < 0.05). MuSK-ab+ MG patients had a higher prevalence of sleep related breathing disorders than the two comparative groups (Odds Ratio [Confidence Interval] 4.97 [1.39-17.82], 3.82 [1.15-12.71], respectively) and for obstructive sleep apnea in MuSK-ab+ gMG vs. MuSK-ab- gMG (4.33 [1.20-15.61]). MuSK-ab+ patients had higher rates of sleep related hypoventilation than MuSK-ab- groups (8.8 [1.01-76.96], 19.46 [2.18-2574]) and requirement for bilevel PAP and nocturnal supplemental oxygen (Odds ratio for both groups, 23.04 [2.63-3037], 23.0 [2.63-3037]). Our cohort suggests MuSK-ab+ patients are more likely to have sleep-related breathing disorders independent of MGFA class, age, and sex. Given the long-term health risks of sleep-related breathing disorders, we suggest clinicians perform routine sleep screening with a low threshold for in-laboratory polysomnography.

items.title: Monocyte-to-HDL Cholesterol Ratio and Complete Blood Count-Derived Inflammatory Markers in Myasthenia Gravis: A Cross-Sectional Case-Control Study.
items.authors: Burak Özaltun, Merve Hilal Ceren Akgör
items.abstract: Background/Objectives: We evaluated the monocyte-to-high-density lipoprotein (HDL) cholesterol ratio (MHR) and complete blood count (CBC)-derived inflammatory ratios in myasthenia gravis (MG). Methods: In this cross-sectional case-control study, 80 patients with MG and 87 controls were compared. MHR, neutrophil-to-lymphocyte ratio (NLR), platelet-to-lymphocyte ratio (PLR), lymphocyte-to-monocyte ratio (LMR), and systemic inflammation response index (SIRI) were analyzed with Mann-Whitney U tests, ROC analysis, and multivariable logistic regression with covariates selected using a directed acyclic graph. Results: MHR was higher in MG (median 0.0091 vs. 0.0058; q < 0.001), as were NLR, PLR, and SIRI, whereas LMR was lower. AUCs were 0.779 (SIRI), 0.774 (LMR), and 0.700 (MHR). Each 0.001-unit increase in MHR was associated with 1.23-fold higher odds of MG (95% confidence interval 1.11-1.38; p < 0.001), and adding MHR to the covariates increased the model area under the curve from 0.752 to 0.823 ( p = 0.017; complete-case analysis, p = 0.216), mainly through the monocyte count. No marker correlated with severity (all p > 0.12). Conclusions: MHR and CBC-derived ratios differed between patients with MG and controls independent of demographic and metabolic covariates, largely reflecting monocyte counts, but were not associated with severity and do not appear suitable for disease monitoring.

items.authors: Tsukasa Kato, Ken Miura, Hiroyuki Watanabe
items.abstract: Anti-Kv1.4 antibody-associated myocarditis is an extremely rare condition and its optimal long-term management remains unclear. A 66-year-old woman presented with myasthenia gravis-like symptoms, marked creatine kinase elevation, leukopenia, and hypogammaglobulinaemia. She developed acute myocarditis with ventricular arrhythmias and a reduced left ventricular ejection fraction. Intravenous immunoglobulin and corticosteroid therapy resulted in rapid clinical and cardiac improvement. During cautious tapering of oral prednisolone, she was readmitted with febrile neutropenia and subsequently developed progressive ventricular dysfunction and cardiogenic shock. Cardiac magnetic resonance imaging demonstrated extensive myocardial fibrosis, and autopsy revealed diffuse lymphocytic infiltration. Post-mortem testing confirmed positivity for anti-Kv1.4 antibodies. This case highlights the potentially fatal course of suspected anti-Kv1.4 antibody-associated inflammatory myocardial disease despite an initial favourable response to immunosuppressive therapy. It illustrates the diagnostic and therapeutic challenges of distinguishing immune-mediated progression from other causes of myocardial injury and implies the need for individualized long-term management strategies.

items.title: From seropositivity to pathogenicity: causal evidence for autoantibodies in myasthenia gravis.
items.authors: Fanxin Kong
items.abstract: Autoantibody testing has expanded the serological spectrum of myasthenia gravis (MG), but detection of disease-associated immunoreactivity does not by itself establish direct pathogenicity. This Review examines how an MG-associated antibody moves from serological observation to mechanistic causality. We organize the evidence around three questions: whether the antibody signal is reproducible and biologically interpretable, whether circulating antibody can engage the native target and produce neuromuscular-junction dysfunction, and whether the resulting phenotype can be attributed to that antibody specificity. Acetylcholine receptor (AChR) and muscle-specific kinase (MuSK) antibodies provide mature causal benchmarks. Low-density lipoprotein receptor-related protein 4 (LRP4) illustrates established pathogenicity despite assay-dependent detection and an incompletely resolved balance between signaling interference, Fc-dependent effects, and local complement injury. Agrin has substantial biological and functional support, but independent sufficiency of human anti-agrin antibodies remains incompletely resolved. Cortactin provides a contrasting example in which repeated serological detection has not been linked convincingly to native target engagement or direct neuromuscular-junction dysfunction. ColQ, rapsyn, and collagen XIII remain unresolved for different reasons. Rather than assigning a numerical pathogenicity score, we identify the specific causal step that is missing for each antibody and match that uncertainty to the most informative experimental approach. This framework may improve interpretation of expanding antibody panels and help prioritize mechanistic studies that distinguish clinically useful biomarkers from directly pathogenic autoantibodies.

items.title: The "Heat-and-Cold" Strategy: Combining Intercostal Nerve Cryoablation for Analgesia After Uniportal VATS Pleurectomy and Hyperthermic Intrathoracic Chemotherapy.
items.authors: Dania Nachira, Giovanni Punzo, Giuseppe Calabrese, Stefano Margaritora, Filippo Lococo
items.abstract: We report interesting images from a 54-year-old woman with recurrent B2 thymoma associated with myasthenia gravis, treated using a minimally invasive uniportal VATS pleurectomy combined with hyperthermic intrathoracic chemotherapy (HITHOC). Preoperative imaging identified two hypermetabolic pleural lesions. Complete resection was achieved, followed by cisplatin-based HITHOC. Postoperative pain was managed by a multimodal approach combining erector spinae plane block and intercostal nerve cryoablation, resulting in a VAS score of two on the first postoperative day, decreasing to zero subsequently, and with no opioid requirement to control pain. The patient experienced an uneventful recovery and rapid discharge. This case highlights the feasibility and safety, with favourable outcomes in this patient. Larger and comparative series are needed to confirm the potential advantages of combining minimally invasive surgery with advanced analgesic strategies in complex thoracic oncology.

items.title: Case Report: Fulminant sintilimab-associated myocarditis complicated by complete atrioventricular block and suspected myositis-myasthenia gravis overlap syndrome.
items.authors: Pian Cheng, Xiaolin Zhao, Min Jin, Qinghua Lai, Jie Liu
items.abstract: Immune checkpoint inhibitor (ICI)-associated myocarditis can cause life-threatening conduction disturbances and may coexist with neuromuscular immune-related adverse events. We report a 67-year-old man with stage IIIA lung squamous cell carcinoma who developed fatigue, bilateral ptosis, myalgia, weakness, and palpitations 13 days after his first dose of sintilimab following concurrent chemoradiotherapy. On admission, cardiac troponin T (cTnT) was 874.2 ng/L and creatine kinase-MB exceeded 300 μg/L. Serial electrocardiograms showed progression from bundle branch and fascicular block to complete atrioventricular block, profound bradycardia, and shock, despite a left ventricular ejection fraction of 54%. Coronary angiography revealed no obstructive coronary disease. The findings supported a clinical diagnosis of sintilimab-associated myocarditis with clinically suspected myositis-myasthenia gravis overlap syndrome; cardiac magnetic resonance imaging and confirmatory neuromuscular investigations were not performed. Treatment included intravenous methylprednisolone, immunoglobulin, mycophenolate mofetil, temporary cardiac pacing, and two limited-volume plasma exchange sessions (600 mL each). Infliximab (300 mg per infusion) was subsequently administered empirically for persistent myocardial biomarker elevation. Sinus rhythm returned, and cardiopulmonary and neuromuscular symptoms improved. Following withdrawal of immunosuppression, chest discomfort recurred alongside a cTnT rise to 299.4 ng/L, prompting resumption of corticosteroid-based therapy. At the latest follow-up on April 30, 2026, the patient remained asymptomatic with stable cardiac function, although cTnT remained mildly elevated. In ICI-associated myocarditis, a preserved ejection fraction does not exclude life-threatening conduction disease, and myocardial injury may recur after immunosuppression is withdrawn; continued ECG and troponin surveillance is therefore warranted.

items.title: Pembrolizumab-Associated Myocarditis and Myasthenic Crisis: Discordant Functional and Tissue Recovery.
items.authors: Allen M Yu, Billal Mohmand, Hend Bcharah, Conor Willson, Abeeha Naqvi, Zachary T Wilson
items.abstract: Immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICI) can cause myocarditis with overlapping neuromuscular toxicity. A 77-year-old man developed biopsy-supported ICI myocarditis with biventricular dysfunction (left ventricular ejection fraction: 36%) after 1 pembrolizumab cycle. The course was complicated by seropositive myasthenia gravis (MG) requiring mechanical ventilation and an unexpected nonocclusive saddle pulmonary embolism. Corticosteroid-refractory troponin elevation prompted escalation to abatacept, while prednisone was reduced for worsening myasthenic weakness. Follow-up cardiac magnetic resonance during sepsis showed improved left ventricular ejection fraction of 53%, but myocardial T2 remained elevated with a persistent nonischemic pattern of late gadolinium enhancement. Troponin remained elevated, and ventilator dependence persisted. ICI myocarditis may show improving ventricular systolic function while myocardial tissue abnormalities persist, and coexisting MG may limit corticosteroid use. Myocarditis and MG may coexist and require multidisciplinary management. Troponin T may remain elevated for months and is not diagnostic of ongoing myocardial inflammation.

items.title: Good's syndrome and infections in a large retrospective cohort of thymoma.
items.authors: Wenji Jia, Lei Jin, Xiao Huan, Chong Yan, Jianying Xi, Liewen Pang, Chongbo Zhao, Jie Song, Xianglin Chu, Sushan Luo
items.abstract: Good's syndrome (GS) is an immunodeficiency associated with thymoma characterized by hypogammaglobulinemia. The co-existence of recurrent infections may be associated with quality of life and overall survival. Despite its relevance, the impact of GS on patients with thymoma has rarely been studied in large cohorts. This is a retrospective cohort study of patients with pathologically confirmed thymoma recruited between May 2010 and November 2024. Data on peripheral immune profile, infections, and paraneoplastic syndrome (PNS) were collected and analyzed. Of 1001 patients with thymoma, we ultimately included 158 patients who underwent peripheral immune profiling. The prevalence of GS was 45.6% (72/158), and the infections were reported in 43.69% (69/158). Infection rates were higher in the GS group than in non-GS group (50% versus 32.72%, P = 0.0384). Among the 121 pathogens identified from this cohort, bacteria were the most prevalent (52.07%, 63/121), followed by fungi (34.71%, 42/121) and virus (13.22%, 16/121). Patients with infections had significantly lower overall survival compared with those without infections (P < 0.001). In addition, patients with multiple PNS had poorer survival than those with a single PNS (P < 0.001). No significant difference in overall survival was found between the GS and the non-GS groups. GS and infections are prevalent in patients with thymoma. Infections and multiple PNS were associated with poorer survival outcomes. These findings highlight the importance of early detection and intervention for improving prognosis and long-term survival in patients with thymoma.
